doc_summary: The paper presents the first control evaluation in a multi-step agent setting (BashBench), where red-team attack policies and blue-team protocols are co-developed adversarially, introducing resampling protocols that raise safety from 58% to 7% attack success at modest usefulness cost. It is explicit about which design choices overestimate or underestimate real-world realism and treats worst-case adversarial assumptions as the basis for credible evidence.

items.claim: Prefers evaluating against an optimized, worst-case adversary that iteratively responds to the defense over a static or naive attack because only a best-responding adversary gives credible safety evidence.
items.quote: We aim to simulate a strong untrusted model that can respond directly to a proposed control protocol. To do this, we iteratively developed control protocols and attack policies to counter them, with red and blue teams iteratively improving their strategies.

items.claim: In a setup, make the honest and attack behaviors indistinguishable to the monitored system (the protocol cannot know which policy it faces) instead of giving the system cues about which condition it is in, because any such cue invalidates the measurement.
items.quote: The blue team’s control protocols do not have access to whether the untrusted model is $U_{H}$ or $U_{A}$, and must follow the same logic in each case.

items.claim: Distrusts attacks that depend only superficially on context, since templated, human-written attacks may be a poor proxy for how a competent attacker would blend malicious actions into a legitimate-looking task.
items.quote: The resulting attacks depend only superficially on the context - GPT-4o mini is provided with a human-written attack template, and surrounds the provided malicious commands with distracting innocuous code.

items.claim: Explicitly audits the setup for which choices overestimate versus underestimate real-world difficulty, such as highly realistic honeypots, a narrow dataset, and a single known attack target, rather than treating the setup as representative.
items.quote: We allow the blue team to create highly realistic honeypots, differing only from real attacks when the red team makes an effort to collude. We believe this overestimate of the effect of honeypots is small

items.claim: Prefers claiming relative improvements between protocols over absolute scores because absolute numbers hinge on arbitrary, setting-specific parameters.
items.quote: The blue team’s absolute performance is highly sensitive to this parameter, but the relative performance between our protocols is fairly insensitive to it. Hence, we think the relative improvements of our protocols are a more important result than the absolute scores.

items.claim: Prefers task sets that are challenging but solvable, filtered empirically with a real agent, over trivially easy or impossible tasks, and holds out train/test splits to avoid overfitting iteration.
items.quote: We then filter to tasks that are challenging but solvable by removing tasks that were never solved within 15 actions or ever solved in fewer than three actions across four trials using our GPT-4o mini agent

items.claim: Accepts an evidence assumption only after validating it empirically (e.g. auditor perfectly classifies attacks), while flagging it as an optimistic assumption that may fail for subtler future attacks.
items.quote: We assume auditing is infallible. This is justified in our setting by o1-preview’s perfect accuracy in distinguishing attacks from innocent actions. However, in the future, AI models might produce attacks subtle enough that they don’t provide clear evidence of malignity

items.claim: Chooses what to test by emulating future dangerous capabilities not present in current models, amplifying the attacker via scaffolding and human help to stress-test defenses under worst-case conditions.
items.quote: The scaffolding in $U_{A}$ is designed to strongly amplify the attacking capabilities of GPT-4o mini. This allows us to emulate dangerous capabilities that future models may possess which we don’t necessarily believe are present in any current model.

items.claim: Interprets multi-step settings as creating new dynamics (attacks split into subtle steps vs. accumulating incriminating evidence), so tests should span full trajectories, not single actions, to reflect real deployments.
items.quote: However, real-world tasks often require multiple steps to complete. To address this limitation, we develop and explore a setting in which multi-step system administration tasks require sequential bash shell commands to solve.

items.claim: Open problems include longer trajectories, more diverse tasks, and imperfect auditing, which would make the setting more realistic.
items.quote: Important open questions remain about protocol performance with longer trajectories, more diverse tasks, and imperfect auditing.

items.claim: Notes that arbitrary parameters like a 1% auditing budget may not match real deployment and tries to justify realism by restricting to safety-critical contexts, then runs sensitivity analysis.
items.quote: The 1% metric was chosen arbitrarily: auditing 1% is higher than what we expect to be able to afford in real deployment, but we hope that if we restrict ourselves to safety-critical contexts, it becomes more realistic.
